subject: Scaling a questionnaire over the years

messages.author: 9403604069d4685f
messages.subject: Scaling a questionnaire over the years
parts:
Dear Phil,

I am working with some questionnaires from several datasets that contain data collected for a long timespan (10 to 40 years). In some datasets, the responses were collected in a longitudinal manner and in some in a cross-sectional manner.

I have analyzed the data using both confirmatory factor analysis and item response theory. These analyses tell me that there is no measurement invariance. In other words, CFA tells me that the factor loadings change over the years of questionnaire administartion (they tend to increase), while IRT tells me that the item parameters also change over the years.

The papers that I have read tell me that it's not really justifiable to look at how the scores change over the years if there is no measurement invariance over time. However, I was wondering if it may somehow still be possible to do this. One thing that comes to my mind is scaling using IRT, which I know that I can do using your mirt package using the multipleGroup function in which I would specify the names of anchor items. However, the issue that I have is that there are no anchor items, or to put it more straightforward, all items are anchor items - the questionnaire did not change over the years. Therefore I was wondering if it would make sense to use the multipleGroup function (with the year as a group) and to specify all items as anchor items in order to see how the measured construct changes over the years. I would also free the latent means using mirt.model and then plot the latent means over years.

If this is not the right approach, is there anything you would recommend?

messages.subject: Re: Scaling a questionnaire over the years
parts:
On Sat, Aug 18, 2018 at 11:02 AM AM <mut...@gmail.com> wrote:
Dear Phil,

I am working with some questionnaires from several datasets that contain data collected for a long timespan (10 to 40 years). In some datasets, the responses were collected in a longitudinal manner and in some in a cross-sectional manner.

I have analyzed the data using both confirmatory factor analysis and item response theory. These analyses tell me that there is no measurement invariance. In other words, CFA tells me that the factor loadings change over the years of questionnaire administartion (they tend to increase), while IRT tells me that the item parameters also change over the years.

How does this tell you there is no measurement invariance? If the properties of the population change, such as there is more variability in the latent trait distribution/mean-score increases, then changes in the observed item parameters would be expected. It's only possible to make this type of conclusion if you are certain the population latent trait values themselves should theoretically remain constant over time; otherwise, you'd have to do some item parameter equating.

The papers that I have read tell me that it's not really justifiable to look at how the scores change over the years if there is no measurement invariance over time. However, I was wondering if it may somehow still be possible to do this. One thing that comes to my mind is scaling using IRT, which I know that I can do using your mirt package using the multipleGroup function in which I would specify the names of anchor items. However, the issue that I have is that there are no anchor items, or to put it more straightforward, all items are anchor items - the questionnaire did not change over the years. Therefore I was wondering if it would make sense to use the multipleGroup function (with the year as a group) and to specify all items as anchor items in order to see how the measured construct changes over the years. I would also free the latent means using mirt.model and then plot the latent means over years.

If this is not the right approach, is there anything you would recommend?

Unfortunately, I don't think I'd recommend this 100%, unless under special conditions. The longitudinal aspect of the model suggests that individuals appeared in more than one time point, while in multipleGroup() the individuals are assumed to be independent. More than likely you'd have to setup some type of longitudinal model, like so: https://philchalmers.github.io/mirt/html/Longitudinal-IRT.html. This example isn't the best in that the constraints use an older format (I should replace it with the current syntax mode....but haven't found the time yet), so you'll have to try to determine what's going on from the output coefficients. Similar analyses are also possible with SEM, and if you can make the assumption that the items types are strictly ordinal (so that the graded response model is reasonable) then it may be best to start with that method before moving to IRT, primarily for estimation-based reasons. HTH.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: Scaling a questionnaire over the years
parts:
Dear Phil,

Thank you for the examples. I will do my best to produce such models and apply them to my data. However, I am a bit confused about the answer and I was trying to wrap my head around it. If the population-mean score of the latent trait is increasing, shouldn't that only impact the person parameter (Theta) and not the item parameters? Isn't one of the advantages of IRT over CTT that the person parameters and item parameters are independent? In other words, if the item parameters change over the years, doesn't that tell us that the very way in which people respond to items has changed (and not necessarily the person parameters/population means)?

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: Scaling a questionnaire over the years
parts:
Just because the item parameters and latent trait values are independent does not mean that their scale is constant. This is why IRT models often set the latent trait identification to have a mean of 0, variance of 1 (same problem occurs in SEM). If some other values were chosen then these would in fact affect the item parameters. This is actually the reason why *linking* parameter sets across multiple groups is required, because any mean/variance differences will make the parameters non-equivalent. 

If you are still having trouble with this idea, consider playing around with the example code in the multipleGroup() function, generating data with different latent trait distributions, and see how the single group item parameters can change. Also, topics on DIF will illuminating as well. HTH. 

Phil
